title: Florida's Condominium Ombudsman: what the office can do for owners and boards, and what it can't
seoTitle: Florida Condo Ombudsman: What the Office Can and Can't Do
description: Florida has a state Condominium Ombudsman for owners and boards. Here is what the office does, how election monitors work, and how to reach it.
dek: When a condo dispute won't settle at the board table, many owners don't know there is a state office set up to be a neutral go-between. Here is what it does, what it doesn't, and how to reach it.

body.text: Sooner or later, many condo owners hit a wall. Maybe it is a dispute about an election, a meeting, or a neighbor. The board says one thing, the owner says another, and nobody wants to hire a lawyer over it.

Florida has a state office for moments like this: the Office of the Condominium Ombudsman. Many owners have never heard of it. This article explains, in plain words, what the 2026 Florida Statutes say the office can do, what it is not set up to do, and how to reach it. It is a guide, not legal advice.

body.title: Terms to know
body.text: Ombudsman: an official whose job is to help people with a government system and to help settle disputes. Division: the Division of Florida Condominiums, Timeshares, and Mobile Homes, part of the Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR). It is the state agency that regulates condo associations. Total voting interests: all the votes in the association, usually one per unit, counting every unit, not just the owners who show up. Election monitor: a neutral person appointed to attend the annual meeting and run the board election.
Where the office sits and who runs it

Section 718.5011 of Florida law creates the office. For administrative purposes it sits inside the Division. The ombudsman is a bureau chief of the Division and is paid for out of the Division's trust fund, like other Division bureaus.

The Secretary of DBPR appoints the ombudsman, who serves at the pleasure of the Governor. The law bars the ombudsman and full-time staff from outside work that conflicts with the office's duties, and from certain political party and campaign activity.
The office is based in Fort Lauderdale, but it serves condo owners and boards statewide.
What the law says the office can do
Section 718.5012 lists the ombudsman's powers. In plain words, the office can:

items: Use the Division's files and records to do its work.
Act as a go-between among the Division, owners, boards, board members, community association managers and others, and prepare educational materials on everyone's rights and responsibilities.

Monitor and review procedures and disputes about condo elections and meetings. If there is reasonable cause to believe election misconduct happened, it can recommend that the Division pursue enforcement. It may also review secret ballots cast in association votes.
Encourage and arrange voluntary meetings among owners, boards, managers and others to settle a dispute inside the community before anyone takes a formal or administrative step.
Help resolve disputes between owners and the association, or between owners, when the matter is not within the Division's power to resolve.
Provide resources to help board members and officers do their jobs.
Send reports and recommendations to the Governor, DBPR, the Division, the Advisory Council on Condominiums, the Senate President and the House Speaker, including ideas for changes in the law.

body.text: The law says the Legislature means for the ombudsman to be "a neutral resource for both the rights and responsibilities of unit owners, associations, and board members." That last part matters. The office is not the owners' lawyer, and it is not the board's lawyer either.
What it is not set up to do

Look closely at the verbs in the law: monitor, recommend, encourage, assist. The statute does not list a power for the ombudsman to fine an association, remove a director, or overturn a board's vote. On elections, the office recommends enforcement; the Division is the agency that would bring it.

The meetings it arranges are voluntary. Nobody can be forced to come or to agree. And the ombudsman is a state office, not a private attorney, so for advice about your own rights in a specific dispute, an attorney is still the person to ask. If you want the state to investigate a possible violation of the condo law, that goes through the Division's complaint process.
Election monitors: owners can ask for one

One of the office's most concrete tools is the election monitor. Under section 718.5012(10), owners holding 15 percent of the total voting interests, or six unit owners, whichever is greater, can petition the ombudsman to appoint a monitor for the association's annual meeting and board election.

Here is a quick example of "whichever is greater." In a 20-unit building with one vote per unit, 15 percent is 3 votes, so six owners are needed. In a 200-unit building, 15 percent is 30 votes, so 30 are needed.

The ombudsman picks the monitor from a Division employee, a person who specializes in condo election monitoring, or a Florida-licensed attorney. The association pays all costs of the monitoring, which means every owner shares that bill. The petition form is DBPR Form CO 6000-9, "Petition for Appointment of Election Monitor," linked from the ombudsman's page on the DBPR website. The Division's rule sets how appointments work, so check the form's instructions for timing before the annual meeting.
How to reach the office

According to DBPR's website, the office can be reached by email at ombudsman@myfloridalicense.com or by phone at 954-202-3234 (954-202-3235 for Spanish). Its mailing address is 1400 W. Commercial Boulevard, Suite 185-J, Fort Lauderdale, FL 33309-3791. DBPR's appointment page also lets people book a virtual meeting with the ombudsman's office over Microsoft Teams.
What to do
If you are an owner:

items: Write down the problem first: dates, notices, minutes and what you asked the board. Clear facts make any call more useful.
Try the board in writing before you go to the state. Many disputes end there.
If talking has stalled, contact the ombudsman's office and ask whether a voluntary meeting could help.
If you are worried about how the next election will be run, talk with your neighbors about the election monitor petition, and remember the association pays the cost.
If you believe the condo law was broken and want the state to look into it, use the Division's complaint process. For advice on your own rights, ask an attorney.

body.text: If you are a board member:

items: Know the office is there for boards too. It can provide resources for directors and officers.
If a dispute with an owner keeps coming back, consider whether a voluntary meeting arranged by the ombudsman's office could cool it down before it becomes a formal case.
If owners file an election monitor petition, ask the association attorney how the process works and plan for the cost in the budget.
Keep election records, notices and ballots in order. A monitor, or the ombudsman reviewing secret ballots, will look at the paper trail.

faq.q: What does the Florida condo ombudsman do?
faq.a: Under section 718.5012 of Florida law, the office acts as a neutral go-between among owners, boards, managers and the state's Division of Condominiums. It monitors election and meeting disputes, can recommend enforcement for election misconduct, arranges voluntary meetings to settle disputes, and can appoint an election monitor when owners petition.

faq.q: Can the condo ombudsman make my board do something?
faq.a: The law gives the office tools like recommendations, voluntary meetings and election monitors. It does not list a power to fine an association, remove a director or overturn a board vote. Enforcement for election misconduct is something the ombudsman can recommend to the Division.

faq.q: How do I contact the Florida condo ombudsman?
faq.a: DBPR's website lists email ombudsman@myfloridalicense.com and phone 954-202-3234 (954-202-3235 for Spanish). The office is at 1400 W. Commercial Boulevard, Suite 185-J, Fort Lauderdale, FL 33309-3791, and virtual meetings can be booked through DBPR's appointment page.

faq.q: How many owners does it take to get an election monitor for a Florida condo?
faq.a: Owners holding 15 percent of the total voting interests, or six unit owners, whichever is greater, can petition the ombudsman using DBPR Form CO 6000-9. The association pays all costs of the monitoring.

faq.q: Is the condo ombudsman the same as filing a complaint with DBPR?
faq.a: No. The ombudsman is a neutral resource that helps people talk and settle disputes. A request for the state to investigate a possible violation of the condo law goes through the Division's complaint process.
